# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. value.markup:

value.markup:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a fragile screen-scraping hack there. With MCP, an AI agent connects once and discovers what a server can do at runtime — no glue code, no hard-coded endpoints.

What makes that awesome is the network effect. Any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so a protocol written once benefits every assistant and every product on both sides of the wire.

values.value: A pragmatic agent
If the only tool you have is a chat window, every problem looks like a prompt. Give the chat window real tools, and every problem starts to look solvable.

value.markup: For a CMS like Umbraco the impact is concrete. This entire site — document types, data types, templates, media, content — was created over the MCP server in a single working session. No migration scripts, no hand-written SQL, no click-throughs in the backoffice. The agent models, then creates, then publishes, exactly as a developer would, but through a formal interface instead of a screen.

values.value: The Model Context Protocol turns an AI assistant from a spectator into a coworker — and this site is the proof.
Why MCP Is Awesome
One protocol, every tool, zero glue code.

value.markup:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a fragile screen-scraping hack there. With MCP, an AI agent connects once and discovers what a server can do at runtime — no glue code, no hard-coded endpoints.

What makes that awesome is the network effect. Any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so a protocol written once benefits every assistant and every product on both sides of the wire.

values.value: A pragmatic agent
If the only tool you have is a chat window, every problem looks like a prompt. Give the chat window real tools, and every problem starts to look solvable.

value.markup: For a CMS like Umbraco the impact is concrete. This entire site — document types, data types, templates, media, content — was created over the MCP server in a single working session. No migration scripts, no hand-written SQL, no click-throughs in the backoffice. The agent models, then creates, then publishes, exactly as a developer would, but through a formal interface instead of a screen.

values.value: A black circuit board — every trace a contract between two components. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash.

value.markup: And because the protocol is open, the same setup works in CI, in local development, or inside your favourite assistant. That is what awesome looks like in practice: less plumbing, more shipping.

values.value: How a small protocol turned a headless backoffice into a place an agent can genuinely work in.
MCP: The Missing Link Between Agents and Your CMS
How a small protocol turned a headless backoffice into a place an agent can genuinely work in.

value.markup:
Every integration between an AI assistant and another system used to start the same way: reverse-engineer the UI, guess at the API, hard-code the calls. MCP replaces that ritual with a contract. A server declares its tools with typed inputs and outputs; the client asks what's available; the model plans against what it actually finds.

That last part matters most. A protocol that advertises its own capabilities turns a static integration into a conversation: the agent can ask a question, get a typed answer, and decide what to do next on its own.

values.value: A connected structure seen from below — every node one call away. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.
Umbraco.Bench
An agent is only as useful as the surfaces it can safely touch.

value.markup: Umbraco's MCP server is a working proof. It speaks the management API, so an agent can create document types, wire up block grids, upload media, publish content — the same operations an editor performs by hand. When the protocol enforces the rules, working through it is as safe as working in the backoffice itself, and a great deal faster.

values.value: The Model Context Protocol turns an AI assistant from a spectator into a coworker — and this site is the proof.
Why MCP Is Awesome
One protocol, every tool, zero glue code.

value.markup:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a fragile screen-scraping hack there. With MCP, an AI agent connects once and discovers what a server can do at runtime — no glue code, no hard-coded endpoints.

What makes that awesome is the network effect. Any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so a protocol written once benefits every assistant and every product on both sides of the wire.

values.value: A pragmatic agent
If the only tool you have is a chat window, every problem looks like a prompt. Give the chat window real tools, and every problem starts to look solvable.

value.markup: For a CMS like Umbraco the impact is concrete. This entire site — document types, data types, templates, media, content — was created over the MCP server in a single working session. No migration scripts, no hand-written SQL, no click-throughs in the backoffice. The agent models, then creates, then publishes, exactly as a developer would, but through a formal interface instead of a screen.

values.value: A black circuit board — every trace a contract between two components. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash.

value.markup: And because the protocol is open, the same setup works in CI, in local development, or inside your favourite assistant. That is what awesome looks like in practice: less plumbing, more shipping.

values.value: How a small protocol turned a headless backoffice into a place an agent can genuinely work in.
MCP: The Missing Link Between Agents and Your CMS
How a small protocol turned a headless backoffice into a place an agent can genuinely work in.

value.markup:
Every integration between an AI assistant and another system used to start the same way: reverse-engineer the UI, guess at the API, hard-code the calls. MCP replaces that ritual with a contract. A server declares its tools with typed inputs and outputs; the client asks what's available; the model plans against what it actually finds.

That last part matters most. A protocol that advertises its own capabilities turns a static integration into a conversation: the agent can ask a question, get a typed answer, and decide what to do next on its own.

values.value: A connected structure seen from below — every node one call away. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash.
Umbraco.Bench
An agent is only as useful as the surfaces it can safely touch.

value.markup: Umbraco's MCP server is a working proof. It speaks the management API, so an agent can create document types, wire up block grids, upload media, publish content — the same operations an editor performs by hand. When the protocol enforces the rules, working through it is as safe as working in the backoffice itself, and a great deal faster.

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a fragile screen-scraping hack there. With MCP, an AI agent connects once and discovers what a server can do at runtime — no glue code, no hard-coded endpoints.

What makes that awesome is the network effect. Any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so a protocol written once benefits every assistant and every product on both sides of the wire.

values.value: The Model Context Protocol turns an AI assistant from a spectator into a coworker — and this site is the proof.
Why MCP Is Awesome
One protocol, every tool, zero glue code.

value.markup:
The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets applications expose tools, resources and prompts to AI assistants in a uniform way. Before MCP, every integration was bespoke: a custom plugin here, a fragile screen-scraping hack there. With MCP, an AI agent connects once and discovers what a server can do at runtime — no glue code, no hard-coded endpoints.

What makes that awesome is the network effect. Any MCP client can talk to any MCP server, so a protocol written once benefits every assistant and every product on both sides of the wire.

values.value: A pragmatic agent
If the only tool you have is a chat window, every problem looks like a prompt. Give the chat window real tools, and every problem starts to look solvable.

value.markup: For a CMS like Umbraco the impact is concrete. This entire site — document types, data types, templates, media, content — was created over the MCP server in a single working session. No migration scripts, no hand-written SQL, no click-throughs in the backoffice. The agent models, then creates, then publishes, exactly as a developer would, but through a formal interface instead of a screen.

values.value: A black circuit board — every trace a contract between two components. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash.

value.markup: And because the protocol is open, the same setup works in CI, in local development, or inside your favourite assistant. That is what awesome looks like in practice: less plumbing, more shipping.
